```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = FALSE)
```

MCP Console gives an LLM agent an R session, with a sandbox to limit what its code can do on your machine.
The agent can write R code, inspect the results, and follow up in the same session.
You can prepare the packages it needs and set limits on where it can write and which services it can contact.

Suppose you'd like a daily email summarizing the latest sales data.
An agent could investigate the data, make a few plots, and explain what changed.
To do that, it needs access to R and the data, but you want to scope that access before leaving it to run unattended.
We'll set up the session and its sandbox permissions, inspect the configuration, then let the agent prepare a report and a summary for your script to send.

The report is our running example, but the same configuration workflow applies to other uses of Console, such as interactive analysis or model evaluations.
The examples below are displayed without execution when this vignette is built.

## Start with explicit settings

First, choose the directory the agent will work in.
Replace `/path/to/report` with an existing directory containing your data.
The R package finds Console automatically.

```{r paths}
library(mcp.console)

project <- normalizePath("/path/to/report", mustWork = TRUE)
```

All relative configuration paths below are relative to `project`.
For example, `./reports` means a directory inside the report project.

For an unattended job, it's useful to state the configuration in the script so you can review it alongside the task.
`ConsoleConfig()` reads no configuration files, and passing it to `console_tools()` skips global and project configuration discovery.

Console uses the R installation running this script by default.
Let's prepare `rmarkdown` and `httr2` for the agent.
The initial sandbox policy lets it write reports and contact an API.
Replace `api.example.com` with the service your report needs.
On Windows, a managed proxy also permits local binding because MXC's host-loopback access is bidirectional.
Explicitly disabling local binding with a managed proxy is unsupported there; see [Windows networking](https://posit-dev.github.io/mcp-console/sandbox_configuration/#unix-sockets-and-local-binding).

```{r config}
config <- ConsoleConfig(
  languages = "r",
  inherit_environment = FALSE,
  environment = c(TZ = "UTC"),
  r = list(
    vanilla = TRUE,
    packages = c("rmarkdown", "httr2")
  ),
  sandbox = list(
    filesystem = list(
      read_only = "./data",
      read_write = "./reports",
      deny = "~/.ssh"
    ),
    network = "api.example.com"
  )
)
```

Console starts a separate R session.
Here, `vanilla = TRUE` skips R startup files, and `packages` lists packages to prepare at startup.
Packages already available in the new session's R libraries can also be used without listing them here.
The default `resolution = "implicit"` lets Console prepare missing packages as the agent loads them, for example with `library()` or `::`.

We also set `inherit_environment = FALSE` so the worker and package resolver don't inherit environment variables from the calling process, such as credentials intended for another service.
The explicit `environment` sets the time zone, and Console supplies its own runtime variables.
The launcher still uses its trusted host environment to locate executables and prepare dependencies.

There is one detail to keep in mind when scoping file access: Console's sandbox allows reads of host files by default.
`read_only = "./data"` does not hide other readable files.
The `deny` entry blocks access to `~/.ssh`; add other sensitive locations as needed.
See [Sandbox permissions](https://posit-dev.github.io/mcp-console/sandbox_configuration/) for the full policy.

Package preparation has separate permissions and may download packages at startup or while the agent is working.
See [Package settings](https://posit-dev.github.io/mcp-console/package_configuration/#preparation-permissions) if you need to configure that access too.

## Add a writable directory and an allowed domain

The report would be easier to read with a sales trend plot.
Let's add a directory for figures while keeping the existing permission to write to `reports/`.
The configuration is an S7 object, so we can edit its properties with `@`:

```{r figures}
`append<-` <- function(x, value) c(x, value)
append(config@sandbox@filesystem@read_write) <- "./figures"
```

Now suppose the report needs a second data source.
We can add its domain to the existing allow list in the same way.
Replace `data.example.com` with that service's hostname:

```{r domain}
append(config@sandbox@network@proxy@domains@allow) <- "data.example.com"
```

This grants access to the hostname; it doesn't restrict individual URL paths or email recipients.

Before starting the session, create the directories where the agent will save its work:

```{r directories}
for (directory in config@sandbox@filesystem@read_write) {
  destination <- file.path(project, directory)
  if (!dir.exists(destination)) {
    stopifnot(dir.create(destination, recursive = TRUE))
  }
}
```

## Review the settings

The object contains the choices we made in R, with the same nested sections as a `config.yaml`.
Review it before launching:

```{r inspect}
print(config)
```

Printing also shows any environment values you included.
The calling R installation supplies the default executable at launch; a configured `r.executable` would take precedence.
Console generates tool descriptions from the current settings when the tools are created.
We can edit permissions or parameter visibility without a separate resolution step.

For example, this hides the optional timeout parameter while retaining its runtime default:

```{r tool-settings}
config@tool <- list(parameters = list(timeout_ms = list(enabled = FALSE)))
```

## Give the agent its tools

With the configuration reviewed, we can start Console and get its tools to register with an [ellmer](https://ellmer.tidyverse.org/) chat:

```{r launch}
tools <- console_tools(config = config, project = project)
```

The sandbox describes what the agent is allowed to do.
The chat prompt describes the work we'd like it to do within those limits.
Let's give it the report task and register the tools so it can use R to investigate the data.
This step requires an ellmer provider and its credentials in the calling R process; this example uses OpenAI.
Those credentials are not forwarded to Console's workers unless you include them in the configuration.

```{r chat}
chat <- ellmer::chat_openai(
  system_prompt = paste(
    "Use the console to prepare the scheduled report.",
    "Read input files from data/ and write the report to reports/.",
    "Write figures to figures/ and explain any missing inputs."
  )
)
chat$register_tools(tools)
```

Now ask for the report.
Replace `data/sales.csv` and the task details with your own inputs and requirements:

```{r report}
summary <- chat$chat(
  paste(
    "Summarize the latest data in data/sales.csv.",
    "Save reports/sales-summary.md and a sales trend plot in figures/.",
    "Return a short summary and the paths of the files you created."
  )
)
cat(summary)
```

Keep `tools` and `chat` reachable until the job finishes.
The agent can use R to inspect the data and save its report and figures, then return a summary to the calling script.
That script can send the summary or report through your existing email workflow, with the recipient specified in your code.

Once you're satisfied with a run, save the code in a script such as `report.R` and have your scheduler run `Rscript --vanilla report.R`.
The calling R installation will remain the default.
You can save an inspected configuration with `saveRDS(config, "report-config.rds")` and load it with `readRDS()`; continue to supply the intended `project` at launch.

If you already keep configuration in files, use that as your starting point:

```{r file-config}
config <- load_console_config(project = project)
# Or read exactly one file yourself, with no discovery:
config <- ConsoleConfig(yaml12::read_yaml("report-config.yaml"))
```

Both return a configuration you can inspect, edit, and launch using the same steps above.
`load_console_config()` accepts `global_file`, `project_file`, and optional R `overrides`.
Setting either source to `NULL` skips it.
`MCP_CONSOLE_HOME` changes the default global file location; project discovery still uses `project/.agents/console/config.yaml`.
Once an object is supplied to `console_tools()`, it discovers no additional config files.
See `?load_console_config` and `?console_tools` for the file and launch options.
